topics.title: Projectile motion — the equation of path

questions.stem: A stone is projected from the origin at 15 m/s and 60° above the horizontal. Its motion is \(x=15t/2\) and \(y=(15\sqrt3/2)t-5t^2\). Show that its path is \(y=\sqrt3x-4x^2/45\).
questions.answer: Sample answer: From \(x=15t/2\), \(t=2x/15\). Substitute this into the vertical equation: \(y=(15\sqrt3/2)(2x/15)-5(2x/15)^2=\sqrt3x-4x^2/45\).
questions.hint: Use the horizontal equation to express t in terms of x, then substitute into the vertical equation.

keyPoints.note: Solve this equation for t before substituting.
Substitute the same t-expression into both terms.

steps.explain: Rearrange the horizontal motion equation to obtain time.

questions.stem: A stone follows the path \(y=\sqrt3x-\frac{4x^2}{45}\). What is its greatest height above the launch point?
questions.hint: The path is a downward-opening quadratic. Find its vertex or set its derivative to zero.

keyPoints.note: The maximum occurs at the vertex of the downward-opening parabola.
Differentiate with respect to x, or use the quadratic vertex formula.

steps.explain: Differentiate the height with respect to horizontal position and set the gradient to zero.

questions.stem: A stone follows \(y=\sqrt3x-\frac{4x^2}{45}\) and lands on the 45° downward slope \(y=-x\). How far down the slope from the origin does it land?
questions.hint: Set the trajectory equal to the slope to find the impact x-coordinate; convert horizontal distance into distance along a 45° line.

keyPoints.note: The impact point is where the projectile path intersects this line.
A 45° slope distance is \(x/\cos45^\circ=x\sqrt{2}\), not just x.

steps.explain: Set the projectile path equal to the slope equation.
Use the nonzero intersection to get the horizontal coordinate.
Convert horizontal distance to length along the 45° slope.

questions.stem: A projectile has the equation of path \(y=-3x^2+2x+4\). How far will it have travelled horizontally before it returns to its original height?
questions.hint: Original height is y(0) = 4; solve y = 4 again.

steps.explain: The original height is the value at \(x=0\).
Find where the height is 4 again.
So \(x=0\) (start) or \(x=\frac23\).
\(\frac13\) is where the projectile is highest (half-way), not where it returns.

keyPoints.note: Original height = y at x = 0. Set y = 4 and solve.

questions.stem:
Zara is testing a batch of homemade bullets on her shooting range.
She holds her rifle at shoulder height (170 cm above the ground) and shoots horizontally with an initial speed of 360 m/s at a target 100m away.
Assume acceleration due to gravity is 10m/s².

parts.hint: Horizontal shot: initial vertical velocity is 0.

steps.explain: Horizontally there is no acceleration; vertically the acceleration is \(-10\).
Integrate. The shot is horizontal, so at \(t=0\): \(\dot x=360\) and \(\dot y=0\).

keyPoints.note: The shot is horizontal, so horizontally means ẏ = 0 and ẋ = 360 at t = 0.

parts.hint: Integrate ẋ and ẏ; the starting height is 1.7 m.

steps.explain: Integrate again, with the origin on the ground below the rifle: \(x=0\) and \(y=1.7\) (170 cm = 1.7 m) at \(t=0\).
Keep units in metres: 170 cm must become 1.7 m.

keyPoints.note: Integrate once more; at t = 0, x = 0 and y = 1.7 (metres, not centimetres).

parts.stem: Hence find the equation of path as \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

steps.explain: From \(x=360t\), make \(t\) the subject.
Substitute into \(y\).

keyPoints.note: Eliminate t: t = x/360, then substitute into y.

parts.stem: Assuming the ground is horizontal at her range, how far above the ground will the bullet hit the target? Give your answer correct to the nearest cm.
parts.hint: Put x = 100 into the path equation.

steps.explain: The target is at \(x=100\).
To the nearest cm:
0.39 m is the drop, not the height.

parts.stem: When does the bullet hit her target? Find the impact speed (correct to 5 significant figures).

steps.explain: Time: from \(x=360t\) at \(x=100\).
Velocity components at that time.
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity.
Adding the components (\(360+2.78\)) is wrong — use Pythagoras.

questions.stem:
A ball is struck by a racquet from a point \(A\) which has position vector \(21\mathbf{j}\) metres relative to a fixed origin \(O\). Initially, the velocity vector of the ball is \((5\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})\) m/s, where \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) are the unit vectors in the horizontal and vertical directions respectively.

After being struck, the ball undergoes projectile motion under the influence of gravity only, that is, the acceleration vector of the ball \(\mathbf{a}=-10\mathbf{j}\). The ball will hit the ground at point \(B\), a point that is on the same horizontal level as the origin.

parts.stem: Show that the velocity vector of the ball \(t\) seconds after being struck is \(\mathbf{v}=5\mathbf{i}+(8-10t)\mathbf{j}\).

steps.explain: Integrate the acceleration component by component.
Use \(\mathbf v(0)=5\mathbf i+8\mathbf j\).
So

parts.answer: Integrate \(\mathbf a=-10\mathbf j\): \(\mathbf v=c_1\mathbf i+(-10t+c_2)\mathbf j\). At t = 0, \(\mathbf v=5\mathbf i+8\mathbf j\) ⇒ c₁ = 5, c₂ = 8. So \(\mathbf v=5\mathbf i+(8-10t)\mathbf j\).

keyPoints.note: Integrate each component of the acceleration, then use the initial velocity.

parts.stem: Find an expression for the position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) of the ball relative to \(O\) at a time \(t\) seconds after it was struck.

steps.explain: Integrate the velocity.
At \(t=0\) the ball is at \(A\): \(\mathbf r(0)=21\mathbf j\).
So

keyPoints.text: Find an expression for the position vector
keyPoints.note: The starting position is 21j: the 21 goes in the j-component.

parts.stem: Find the maximum height that the ball reaches.
parts.hint: Vertical velocity is zero at the top.

steps.explain: At the maximum height the vertical velocity is zero.
Substitute into the vertical position.
3.2 m is only the rise above \(A\).

keyPoints.note: Set the j-component of velocity to zero, then find the j-component of position.

parts.stem: Find the speed of the ball when it lands at \(B\) and the angle at which the ball strikes the ground.
parts.hint: Solve y = 0 for t, then use the velocity at that time.

steps.explain: The ball lands when the vertical position is 0.
Velocity at \(t=3\).
Speed is the magnitude.
The angle with the ground: \(\tan\alpha=\frac{\text{vertical}}{\text{horizontal}}\).
13° would be the angle with the vertical; \(\sqrt{89}\) is the launch speed.

options: \(\sqrt{89}\approx9.43\) m/s at about \(58^\circ\) to the horizontal
\(\sqrt{509}\approx22.56\) m/s at about \(77^\circ\) to the horizontal
\(\sqrt{509}\approx22.56\) m/s at about \(13^\circ\) to the horizontal
\(27\) m/s at about \(77^\circ\) to the horizontal

keyPoints.text: the angle at which the ball strikes the ground
keyPoints.note: Find t when the height is 0, then tan α = |vertical| / horizontal velocity.
